title: Insurance Eligibility Verification Software: Clearinghouses, Services and Portal Automation Compared
summary: Compare clearinghouses, managed verification services and payer-portal automation. Learn where Skyvern fits when electronic eligibility checks leave gaps.
body_markdown:
[HIPAA was passed in 1996](https://aspe.hhs.gov/reports/health-insurance-portability-accountability-act-1996?ref=skyvern.com) , beginning the move toward national standards for electronic healthcare transactions, including[X12 270/271 eligibility inquiries and responses](https://www.cms.gov/priorities/key-initiatives/burden-reduction/administrative-simplification/transactions/health-plan-eligibility-benefit-inquiry-response?ref=skyvern.com) .


The standard is more than twenty years old now, but an electronic check can still come back without what the front desk needs for the visit, like the copay or a visit limit. Someone has to go and get it.


That's the buying decision I want to help you make with insurance eligibility verification software: who completes the check and gets the answer into the appointment record?


At[Skyvern](https://www.skyvern.com/healthcare) , our position is to keep electronic checks that return what you need and[automate the browser work that remains](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/automating-healthcare-insurance-eligibility-verification/) .


In this piece, I'm comparing clearinghouses, managed verification services and payer-portal automation, so you can choose a combination with clear responsibility for unfinished checks.


## What is insurance eligibility verification?


Insurance eligibility verification is the check a provider makes before a visit to confirm that a patient's coverage is active and what the plan will pay toward that visit, such as the copay, the deductible and any visit limits.


## What platforms are used for insurance eligibility verification?


There are three kinds of platforms for verifying insurance eligibility:


- **Clearinghouse or API:** gives you an electronic answer.
- **Managed verification service:** hands the check to a team that finishes it.
- **Payer-portal automation:** logs into the payer's portal and pulls the answer for you.


To pick between them, you need to ask what the front desk needs in hand before this patient walks in.


Approach Best fit What you should get back What to ask


Clearinghouse or API (270/271) The electronic response already has what the visit needs Coverage dates, copay and deductible, with gaps flagged Who can see the results? What do transactions, integration and follow-up cost?


Managed verification service Electronic checks leave gaps that need a portal visit or a phone call A finished benefits record, or an open item with a reason Who enters the result and who follows up? What access does the service get, and what do extra charges cover?


Payer-portal automation The same portal checks repeat and you're authorized to use the portal The portal fields you asked for, or the reason they couldn't be pulled Does the payer allow this use? Who fixes the workflow when the portal changes?

## When are clearinghouse and API 270/271 checks enough?


A clearinghouse or payer API is enough when the response gives your team every benefit the visit needs and your system records it where staff will see it.


### Understanding API 270 and 271


A 270 is the eligibility question and a 271 is the answer.


The[CMS HETS companion guide](https://www.cms.gov/files/document/current-hets-270-271-companion-guide.pdf?ref=skyvern.com) lays out these transactions for Medicare. It treats a patient who doesn't match as an error, separate from a coverage result. It also says a 271 isn't a promise of payment. So when the patient doesn't match, you'd leave the check open and follow up.


### How to test a response


To begin with, write down the fields you require and compare real responses against that list.


Say a patient is booked for physical therapy. The 271 says active coverage but never mentions the visit limit. The check succeeded, and the front desk still can't answer the patient's question.


Speed doesn't settle it either. CAQH CORE's current eligibility rule, vEB.2.0, says a[real-time 271 must come back within 20 seconds](https://www.caqh.org/hubfs/drupal/CAQH%20CORE%20Eligibility%20%20Benefit%20(270_271)%20Infrastructure%20Rule%20vEB.2.0.pdf?ref=skyvern.com) of the 270. A fast response can still leave out the benefit you need.


### Who sells electronic checks


Among the insurance verification software above, pVerify, Inovalon and eClaimStatus sell electronic checks, and each one connects to payers in its own way.


A portal isn't always the better source. UnitedHealthcare[documents portal, API and EDI options](https://www.uhcprovider.com/en/patient-eligibility-benefits.html?ref=skyvern.com) for eligibility and benefits. Before you add browser automation, it's worth finding out which channel works for your task.


## When does a managed verification service fit?


A managed service fits when electronic checks leave gaps and you'd rather hand off the chasing than staff it. Its team picks up what the EDI transaction lacks, through payer portal logins and direct phone calls.


Buying access to a transaction and buying a finished verification are two different deals. So you'll want the finished check in the contract, and four things settled before you sign:


- **Completion:** Which benefits must the service get, and how does it mark what it couldn't find?
- **Turnaround:** How long before the appointment must the record be ready?
- **Escalation:** Who handles an ambiguous match, conflicting benefits, or a payer that wants another call?
- **Delivery:** Who enters the result in your system, and how does staff see that follow-up is still open?


What matters most is how a service handles a failed check, not its payer list, so ask to see both a finished record and an unresolved one. Our[healthcare BPO and automation guide](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/healthcare-bpo/) covers how to split repeated browser work from human follow-up.


## When should payer-portal automation complement eligibility software?


Portal automation makes sense when the electronic check leaves fields open and a portal you're authorized to use has them. That's the browser work Skyvern handles, and we don't try to replace 270/271.


It usually comes up in two situations:


- **The response is incomplete.** The 271 comes back, but a benefit you need isn't in it.
- **There's no usable electronic response.** The payer has none for what you need, so an authorized portal may be your only digital route.


Staff may still have to call when the portal comes up empty too.


With Skyvern, a workflow can:


- Sign into a payer portal.
- Enter the member's details.
- Go to the benefits page.
- Pull the fields you asked for.


Your integration supplies the appointment details and receives the result. You[configure the workflow](https://www.skyvern.com/docs/cloud/studio) and test it one payer at a time.


Scripted bots break when a portal changes its pages. Our post on[agentic automation versus RPA](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/apa-vs-rpa-automation/) explains why, and our[operations guide to agentic automation](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/what-is-agentic-automation-ops-guide/) covers how AI handles browser tasks more generally.


For eligibility, the test is simple: can the workflow pull your required fields from a portal you're allowed to use?


Logins, two-factor prompts and page changes show up in every browser workflow.


Our[credential documentation](https://www.skyvern.com/docs/credentials) is where to start when you plan access. Being able to log in doesn't mean the payer lets you use that account this way, so it's worth reading the payer's terms.


## How do you verify insurance eligibility?


You verify eligibility in five steps, whether you use an electronic connection, a managed service or a portal workflow. It helps to write them down before you compare product demos.


If you already have them as a procedure, our launch-week post shows how to[turn an SOP into a workflow](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/launch-week-day-4-sop-upload-to-build-new-workflows/) :


1. **Collect the inputs.** Patient and subscriber, payer, member ID, rendering provider, planned service and date of service. Decide which benefit fields this appointment needs.
2. **Run the electronic check first.** Use portal or phone follow-up only for what's still missing.
3. **Check the answer.** Is it the right patient and the right visit? Compare the benefits to your required fields. If the patient didn't match, keep the record open and investigate rather than marking coverage inactive.
4. **Record the result.** Save the source, the time of the check, the service date and the benefits on the appointment or registration record. Mark missing fields as missing.
5. **Hand off what's left.** Give every open item an owner and a deadline. Keep[prior authorization](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/automate-healthcare-prior-authorization-insurance-portals/) follow-up separate from the eligibility result.


A blank result shouldn't overwrite an earlier good one, so you'll want to ask each vendor what happens when a run returns nothing.


Our[revenue cycle management automation guide](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/revenue-cycle-management-automation/) shows where eligibility sits in the rest of the revenue cycle.


### How do you use Availity for eligibility verification?


Someone on your team with access runs the check inside[Availity Essentials](https://www.availity.com/multi-payer-portal/?ref=skyvern.com) , a multi-payer portal with real-time eligibility and benefits checks. Availity also lists additional benefit information and patient cost estimates among its eligibility features. It's a portal, so it falls in the portal row of the table and doesn't make a fourth option.


Before you build on it, you'll want to confirm which payers your organization can reach in Availity and what each request needs. Then save the result and its source on the appointment record, so staff can see what's confirmed and what's still open.


## How to evaluate insurance eligibility verification software: security, write-back, cost and exceptions


Once you know which approach fits, the next step is comparing the vendors inside it.


They differ most in five places:


1. payer coverage
2. write-back
3. failure handling
4. patient information
5. cost


The checks below go through each one.


### 1. Payer coverage and benefit detail


You'll want to ask which payer and plan combinations the vendor supports, and for sample responses for your services.


Then sort the fields into three piles: what comes back electronically, what needs the portal and what needs a call.


You also need to know how the team handles real-time checks, advance batch checks and a response that's still incomplete close to the visit. A long payer list tells you little.


### 2. Write-back and integration ownership


Next, watch the result land on the right patient and appointment. Which fields get written? How do partial results show up, and how is existing information protected? Who investigates when a handoff fails?


Our[integrations page](https://www.skyvern.com/integrations) shows what we connect to. Whether your EHR can take eligibility results back is something to scope with us. If your team plans a custom connection, start with our[developer resources](https://www.skyvern.com/developers) and[product documentation](https://www.skyvern.com/docs) .


### 3. When a check fails


Then have the vendor run three failures: an access failure, an unresolved patient match and a response missing a required field.


Each should show a status and who picks it up next. You also need to settle ahead of time who fixes portal changes, and who makes the calls and tells staff a check is unfinished.


For browser automation, ask what logs or screenshots you get when a run fails, who can see them and how long you keep them.


### 4. Patient information and access controls


To begin with, ask each vendor for its signed business-associate agreement, because[HHS explains that](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/covered-entities/sample-business-associate-agreement-provisions/index.html?ref=skyvern.com) HIPAA generally requires business-associate contracts to safeguard protected health information. You need to know which agreements apply to the service you're considering, and you should read them before any patient data goes over.


The[HHS Security Rule summary](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/security/laws-regulations/index.html?ref=skyvern.com) describes role-appropriate access, authentication and audit controls for electronic protected health information. Screenshots, logs and benefit outputs can contain patient information, so they deserve the same review as credentials.


We had an independent SOC 2 audit, and[Skyvern and SOC 2](https://www.skyvern.com/blog/skyvern-x-soc-2/) describes it.


### 5. Total cost


You'll want a quote that breaks out per-check fees, setup, integration, portal maintenance and human review, and a price for a finished check, including the work your staff still does.


We publish our pricing at[skyvern.com/pricing](https://www.skyvern.com/pricing) , and I'd still ask any vendor, us included, for a quote on your own payer mix.


The page price isn't your total cost, because setup and review work add to it. Try asking, "If a check needs a second attempt and a phone call, what do I pay?" A vendor who can't answer in one sentence hasn't priced it.


## Choose the approach that completes your eligibility workflow


Whichever mix you land on, Skyvern covers the part electronic checks leave behind: the portal work.


- **Portal checks, finished.** A workflow signs into the payer portal, pulls the fields you listed and hands them to your integration.
